content: 1. Tuberculosis (TB) cases identified through national prevalence surveys are often at an earlier stage of disease progression compared to those diagnosed in healthcare facilities. This results in a higher likelihood of paucibacillary (low bacterial load) cases being detected. 2. Surveys conducted between 2007 and 2012 revealed that 2–22% of cases included in the final survey results had positive smear microscopy but negative or missing culture results. These cases were included based on a panel review of chest X-rays and smear microscopy findings. 3. The use of Xpert assays (Xpert MTB/RIF or Xpert Ultra) in national TB prevalence surveys between 2011 and 2019 demonstrated higher levels of discordance when compared to culture results. This was particularly evident when Xpert was used alongside culture testing. 4. Between 2015 and 2019, several countries, including Myanmar, Namibia, South Africa, and Vietnam, incorporated Xpert assays into their diagnostic algorithms for TB prevalence surveys. These algorithms varied by country, with some using Xpert for all screen-positive participants and others using culture selectively. 5. In surveys conducted between 2007 and 2016, culture testing generally identified more TB cases than smear microscopy, as expected. Xpert assays were not routinely used in surveys until 2015. 6. The sensitivity and specificity of Xpert assays were evaluated in various settings. For Xpert MTB/RIF, sensitivity was 83% (range: 78–87%), and specificity was 98% (range: 96–99%). For Xpert Ultra, sensitivity was 88% (range: 84–91%) when trace results were considered positive, and specificity was 95% (range: 93–97%). 7. False-positive Xpert results occur because the assay detects DNA from both live and dead TB bacilli, whereas culture requires live bacteria for a positive result. This can lead to discrepancies in TB prevalence surveys, where the goal is to identify active TB disease. 8. Surveys conducted in Lesotho (2019) and South Africa (2017–2019) used both Xpert Ultra and liquid culture (MGIT) for screen-positive individuals. The sensitivity of Xpert Ultra in these surveys was 80% in Lesotho and 78% in South Africa, assuming trace results were positive. 9. The specificity of Xpert assays in prevalence surveys is influenced by the low proportion of culture-positive cases among screen-positive individuals. For example, in surveys conducted between 2007 and 2016, only 1–5% of screen-positive individuals had culture-confirmed TB. 10. The use of two Xpert Ultra tests on separate sputum samples significantly improved sensitivity compared to a single test. In the TREATS study, sensitivity increased from 76% (one sample) to 88% (two samples) when trace results were considered positive. 11. The pooled sensitivity of Xpert Ultra compared to liquid culture was 77% (range: 68–85%), and specificity was 98% (range: 97–99%). Sensitivity was higher among individuals with a history of TB treatment due to the detection of dead bacilli or DNA fragments. 12. The use of Xpert Ultra in surveys has advantages, including rapid results, automation, and reduced risk of cross-contamination. However, its lower sensitivity in detecting early-stage or paucibacillary TB cases in prevalence surveys remains a limitation. 13. The findings from national TB prevalence surveys highlight the importance of combining diagnostic methods, such as Xpert assays and culture, to improve case detection and accurately estimate TB disease burden in the population.
